Guided cloud demos

Source: vignettes/cloud-demos.Rmd
cloud-demos.Rmd

Try an editable Shiny app with your own cloud data platform. The console guide explains where to find the settings, then opens a local app where you sign in and run a query as yourself. The platform enforces your existing permissions. Each example starts with a database identity query, so you don’t need to create tables or upload data.

Choose a platform

Platform name Guide and required setup
"databricks" Databricks: workspace URL and custom OAuth registration; choose a SQL warehouse after sign-in
"fabric" Microsoft Fabric: SQL server/database and an Entra registration; install fabricQueryR, odbc and Microsoft ODBC Driver 18
"bigquery" BigQuery: query project ID and a Google Web OAuth client; no database driver needed
"snowflake" Snowflake: account server, role, warehouse and a confidential custom OAuth integration; install odbc and the Snowflake ODBC driver
"azure-sql" Azure SQL: Entra-enabled server/database and app registration; install odbc and Microsoft ODBC Driver 18
"azure-postgres" Azure PostgreSQL: Entra-enabled server, database, mapped user/group role, trusted CA bundle and app registration; install RPostgres
"redshift" Redshift: IAM Identity Center trusted-token setup with Entra, endpoint/database and delegated API resource/scope; install odbc and AWS Redshift ODBC 2.x
"clickhouse" ClickHouse Cloud: qualifying Enterprise JWT service trusting Entra, HTTPS endpoint and delegated API resource/scope; no database driver needed

For example, start the Fabric guide with:

shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("fabric")

# Open the printed app URL in your regular browser.
# (viewers in RStudio/Positron/etc. cannot perform necessary redirects)

The guide uses cli messages and asks only for missing settings. Enter ? for help, back to revisit a setting, or cancel to save a draft for later. It prints a command to resume the same directory. Account and trial links explain how to arrange access if you have no account yet; eligibility and organization policies still apply. The guide doesn’t provision cloud resources.

All apps run in local R, without Docker. Sign-in doesn’t run SQL; click Run example query when ready. Running queries uses the platform’s normal compute or query allowance. Stop demo ends the local app without stopping shared cloud services. Edit app.R to try different SQL; save and reload the browser. The non-Databricks apps also copy an editable demo-ui.R.

Every platform supports action = "files" to create an offline draft. For scripts, supply the named settings shown in its guide and prompt = FALSE. Settings also use platform-specific environment names, such as OAUTHDB_FABRIC_SERVER or OAUTHDB_FABRIC_TENANT_ID. Secrets use masked input or OAUTHDB_<PLATFORM>_CLIENT_SECRET; the launcher passes them to the child R environment and keeps them out of generated files. Azure platform names use underscores in environment names.

Databricks

With shinyOAuthDB installed, install the optional local-app packages:

install.packages(c("brickster", "jsonlite", "processx", "askpass"))
shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("databricks")

Run this from the R console. The guide uses cli for console messages; you can enter ? for help, back to revisit a setting or cancel to keep a draft. No Docker is needed. Your R code runs on your computer and uses your existing cloud workspace.

Can I use Databricks Free Edition?

Free Edition doesn’t provide the account-console or account-level APIs used to register this custom OAuth app. That blocks this demo’s browser sign-in setup. A full workspace or an eligible full-platform trial needs access to custom OAuth registration. These are different offerings; see Free Edition limits and free trials.

The guide stops early if you select Free Edition. It doesn’t switch to a shared personal token: the purpose is to demonstrate each Shiny visitor’s own OAuth sign-in and data permissions. To try that flow without a cloud account, use the local Docker demos.

Find the sign-in settings

Value Where to find it
Workspace URL Open your workspace and copy its browser address. You can paste the whole URL; the guide keeps only its HTTPS origin.
OAuth client ID Your custom OAuth app registration. The guide can show registration instructions if you don’t have one.
Client secret Only for a confidential registration. Enter it through the masked prompt, or provide OAUTHDB_DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET in your R environment.
Return address The guide supplies http://localhost:8100, or the exact address for your chosen port. Register it without adding a slash or path.

An account administrator creates the registration in Settings > App connections in the Databricks account console. For this SQL example, allow SQL access. The requested scopes are openid, profile, email, offline_access and sql. A public PKCE registration needs no secret; use one for a local demo when your organization permits it. Follow the Databricks registration steps.

The guide supplies a short request to copy to your administrator. If you pause, it prints the draft directory and a command for resuming. It never creates a cloud account, app registration, warehouse or database grant.

If port 8100 is busy, stop the other local app or choose another port:

shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("databricks", port = 8101)

That changes the return address to http://localhost:8101; update the app registration to match. The guide never silently changes a registered callback after sign-in has begun.

Sign in and choose a warehouse

Click Sign in in the local app and use your normal Databricks account. A SQL warehouse is the compute that runs your SQL. After sign-in, the app lists visible warehouses by name and state. Pick one you normally use.

If listing fails or is empty, enter a known warehouse ID or HTTP path from SQL Warehouses > your warehouse > Connection details. You can also supply warehouse_id or http_path when starting the guide. Listing a warehouse doesn’t prove permission to query it; you need CAN USE, and your own tables also need catalog/schema access and appropriate table privileges.

Review the query and click Run example query:

SELECT current_user() AS signed_in_user

Sign-in and warehouse listing don’t open a SQL connection or run this query. Clicking the button does. Queries can start a stopped warehouse and consume normal compute credits; see Databricks’ warehouse behavior. Stopping the local demo doesn’t stop a shared warehouse or change its auto-stop settings.

The warehouse stays fixed for that sign-in after the first query. Sign out and sign in again to choose another one. Sign-out or account changes clear the previous results and selections. The SQL scope doesn’t grant read-only access: the platform still applies the user’s actual privileges.

Edit the app and resume later

The apps use bslib 0.9.0 or later for the sidebar and result panels. The connection panel shows settings relevant to your platform, such as the query project and location in BigQuery, or the role and warehouse in Snowflake. It shows configuration without making extra cloud requests.

The default directory is in R’s user cache, separately for each platform. Your draft survives restarting R: call the same demo again to resume. The launcher prints its location and a command to open the app code. You can also choose a directory:

path <- shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo(
  "databricks",
  action = "files",
  path = "my-databricks-demo",
  prompt = FALSE
)
file.edit(file.path(path, "app.R"))
shinyOAuthDB::oauth_db_cloud_demo("databricks", path = path)

action = "files" works offline and can create an incomplete draft. settings.dcf stores non-secret settings. Existing app.R edits survive later launches. Change example_query to SQL for your own tables, save the file and reload the browser to try it. Back to setup closes the app and opens a console menu of your saved settings. Change a setting by number, enter 0 to continue, or cancel to save and return to R. Your other settings and app edits stay in place. A new workspace or tenant needs its own app registration. Stop demo ends the local process.

To try a fresh copy of the package’s templates, supply a new empty path. The launcher keeps existing files so it won’t overwrite your code.

The launcher passes a confidential secret directly through the child process environment. It doesn’t write it to the project, R command arguments or serialized R files. Tokens stay with shinyOAuth’s session lifecycle. Keep secrets out of app.R, settings.dcf and source control.

For scripted setup, supply host, client_id, client_type and optionally edition, warehouse_id or http_path, with prompt = FALSE. You can also supply OAUTHDB_DATABRICKS_HOST and OAUTHDB_DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID through the environment. A confidential registration uses the secret environment variable above. Missing required values produce an error.

When setup fails

If the workspace check fails, confirm the workspace address and your network/VPN access and trusted TLS certificates. If sign-in reports a redirect mismatch, compare the callback exactly with the registration. An invalid client or scope needs the registration checked; recent registration changes can take time to apply. Use Back to setup to correct app settings, or resume with the printed directory.

A successful sign-in with a failed query usually needs warehouse or data permissions checked. Refresh the list or retry the query explicitly when ready. The demo doesn’t automatically replay SQL after failures.

See Databricks for the complete client and query APIs, and OAuth setup for the underlying sign-in settings.
